extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys and agents), USPTO disciplinary counsel, and attorneys advising clients or practitioners about USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures used by the USPTO tribunal to evaluate alleged misconduct by registered patent practitioners, determine rule violations, assess harm, and select appropriate sanctions (including exclusion). Includes procedural rules for service, default, burden of proof, and aggravating/mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to answer / default consequences (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaint alerted respondent that a decision by default could be entered if a written Answer was not timely filed; in this case respondent's failure to answer resulted in being deemed to have admitted the allegations and entry of default judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by mail and by publication (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: OED must attempt service by mailing the Complaint to addresses reasonably believed to receive mail; if unable to serve by mail, notice may be served by publication in the USPTO Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication requires two consecutive weeks in the Official Gazette; respondent then has thirty days from publication of the second Notice to file an answer. The decision documents examples of returned mail and publication on May 28 and June 4, 2019 making the answer due July 4, 2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary findings and sanction decisions are made based on the OED Director meeting this burden; in default cases admitted allegations are treated as proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and procedures for USPTO disciplinary hearings (37 C.F.R. part 11 subpart C; 5 U.S.C. § 556)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary hearings are conducted in accordance with USPTO's procedural rules at 37 C.F.R. part 11, subpart C, and with section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by a hearing officer appointed by the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative law judges hear cases brought by the USPTO under Interagency Agreement; procedural compliance (service, notices, opportunity to be heard) is required before disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include not filing applications that were hired and paid for, failing to act on time-sensitive Office communications (e.g., Notices of Allowance or Non-Final Rejections), and failing to pursue drafting/filing work after acceptance of compensation. The decision lists multiple client matters where such failures occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to reasonably consult about means (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall 'reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation examples: not informing clients of Notices of Allowance/Abandonment and failing to consult regarding responses to Office notices or available options after abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep clients reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall 'keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide status information to multiple clients (not responding to numerous calls/emails) and failure to forward or notify clients of important Office communications are rule violations shown in the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to promptly comply with reasonable requests for information (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall 'promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision cites repeated failures to respond to clients' telephone calls and requests for status as violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting third-party compensation requires informed consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not accept compensation for representing a client from anyone other than the client unless the client gives informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation example: accepting payment from InventHelp for work for a client without obtaining that client's informed consent about the third-party payor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to promptly deliver funds or property (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall promptly deliver to the client or third person any funds or other property that the client or third person is entitled to receive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include failure to refund unearned fees and retaining filing fees paid for applications that were never filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties upon termination of representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination, a practitioner shall take steps to protect a client's interests, e.g., give reasonable notice, allow time for other counsel, surrender papers/property, and refund unearned advance payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision cites failure to notify clients, failure to return original drawings, and failure to refund unearned fees as violations of this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining advance payments or filing fees for services not performed was characterized as engaging in dishonesty/fraud/deceit in the context of the counts charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duties of patent practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner-client relationship is fiduciary; practitioners owe duties of confidence, trust, and to protect client interests (cited case law and disciplinary precedent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breach examples include accepting payment and then abandoning or neglecting client matters, failing to inform clients of critical Office notices, and failing to return client property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining an appropriate sanction, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these four factors to conclude exclusion is appropriate given multiple rule violations, knowing/negligent conduct, significant actual injury, and aggravating circumstances that outweigh limited mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions — aggravating factors (AM. BAR. ASS'N §§ 9.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards identify aggravating factors (e.g., pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct; indifference to restitution) that justify increased discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision found four aggravating factors present: pattern of misconduct (repeated similar conduct across clients), multiple offenses, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing / lack of remorse, and indifference to making restitution (failure to refund or return property). Prior USPTO cases are cited where these factors resulted in suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions — mitigating factors (AM. BAR. ASS'N §§ 9.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards identify mitigating factors that may reduce discipline (e.g., absence of prior disciplinary record, inexperience in practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision recognized absence of prior disciplinary record and inexperience as mitigating factors but concluded they were insufficient to outweigh aggravation and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual and potential injury to clients as a sanction consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct is a key factor: e.g., abandonment resulting in lost patent rights, shortened patent term, delays in marketing, unrecovered fees, or loss of client property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision documents specific client harms: abandoned applications, funds not refunded, expense to revive applications, and missing original drawings; such injuries support severe sanctions including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior disciplinary precedent and case law as guidance for sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO disciplinary decisions and cited state/federal case law inform interpretation of Rules and appropriate sanctions (e.g., suspension, exclusion) for neglect, abandonment, misappropriation, and failure to communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision cites numerous USPTO precedents (In re Morishita, Shippey, Myers, etc.) and non-USPTO cases to show sanctions historically imposed for similar misconduct and to justify exclusion.
